head:
Foundation · Adherence

Getting started and sticking with it: the real difficulty

Knowing what to do to get fit has never been simpler: the recommendations fit in two lines and are public. Yet a large share of people who start stop, and many of those who want to start never do. This article tests a simple idea: what is missing is less knowledge than patience and repetition. We will see what the research confirms, what it qualifies, and what you can concretely do with it over twelve weeks.

The problem

If you are reading this page, you are on a fitness test. It gives you a starting point in numbers. What comes next is up to you: making something of it, week after week. That is where most plans stop.

People often think: “I don't know where to start, so I do nothing.” Yet what we already know is simple. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, and adds that some activity is better than none.2 It also recommends regular strength training. This foundation is neither secret nor disputed.

And yet, according to the WHO, 31% of adults worldwide, about 1.8 billion people, are not active enough.1 If knowing were enough, this figure would be much lower. Our thesis: knowing what to do is no longer complicated; what is missing is patience and the repetition of the action.

The thesis contains three separate claims: dropping out and never starting are widespread; the obstacle is moving to action and repeating it more than wanting to; “patience” is not a character trait but something that can be organised. Each can be true or false independently of the others.

The question

Is the main obstacle to fitness knowing what to do, or taking action and sticking with it over time? And if it is the second, what actually helps you stick with it, according to the evidence?

Six steps, from the general to the specific: the scale of the problem, the gap between wanting and doing, how long a habit takes, what helps you repeat, the cost of starting and enjoyment, then relapse and objections. The answer and a twelve-week protocol follow.

What is at stake

What is at stake is first of all the simple fact that the benefits of physical activity exist only if the activity exists. The WHO notes that people who are insufficiently active have a 20 to 30% higher risk of death than people who are sufficiently active.1 This is an observed association, not an individual guarantee, but it gives the order of magnitude of what repeated inaction costs over years.

There is also a stake in method: if the real problem is repetition and you treat it as a knowledge problem, you look for the best programme, you change it at every difficulty, and you start again from zero. And if sticking with it can be organised, the first weeks matter more than the programme. This is why this article serves as the foundation for the profile articles: the underlying plan is shared, and what changes from one profile to another is the starting point, the risks and the obstacles.

Step 1 of 6 · The scale of the problem

Starting is common, staying is much less so

We begin with the broadest observation: what happens when inactive adults start an exercise programme? A 1994 review of adherence to exercise programmes, published in Sports Medicine, states the finding right in its abstract: about 50% of people who start an aerobic exercise programme stop within the first six months.3 A 1991 summary document, citing Dishman, gives the same order of magnitude for those who follow their programme alone.4

The review notes that definitions of adherence vary, and that behaviour management programmes seem to improve adherence in the short term (a group of employees exceeded 95% over six months with a set of behavioural techniques).3 Half dropping out is therefore not a law of nature: it depends on how the programme is built.

What this means

For you, this “about 50%” is a benchmark, not a destiny. It comes from old, heterogeneous studies, and does not say why people stop. It establishes the starting fact: the weak point of a plan is what happens after the first weeks, not its content.

The same document associates dropping out with a very high-intensity start, low fitness, overweight, injuries and low self-motivation.4 These are associations drawn from an old summary, not proven causes, but they point to a problem of dose and not only of willpower. This already qualifies the thesis.

Knowing that many people stop does not yet tell us where it breaks down. Do people give up wanting, or do they still want to but fail? The distinction changes everything, and it can be measured.

Step 2 of 6 · The gap between wanting and doing

A large share of people who want to move do not move

The question is precise: among people who say they intend to be active, how many actually are a few weeks later? Rhodes and de Bruijn pooled 10 studies, 3,899 participants, that had measured intention and then observed behaviour afterwards.5

Many people who want to move do not move

Source: Rhodes and de Bruijn, meta-analysis of 10 studies and 3,899 participants, intention measured then physical activity observed later. The 46% gap is published; 36 out of 78 is the direct calculation.

What this means

Out of 100 adults, 78 intended to move. Of these, 42 did and 36 did not, which gives an intention-behaviour gap of 46%. Conversely, almost nobody moves without intending to: 2 out of 100. For you, this means that wanting is almost a necessary condition, but far from a sufficient one. If you have the intention, you are already in the group where the problem plays out, and it plays out in moving to action.

Sheeran and Webb similarly conclude that intentions turn into action about one time in two.6 Across 422 studies (Sheeran 2002), the average correlation between intention and behaviour is 0.53, or about 28% of the variation in behaviour.6,8

Webb and Sheeran pooled 47 randomised trials that increased intention: the effect on intention was medium to large (d = 0.66), the effect on behaviour small to medium (d = 0.36).7 Convincing produces a lot of intention and much less action.

What this means

Motivating is not enough. For you: waiting to “feel motivated” leaves a large part of the road untouched. What matters is what makes the session happen when the desire drops.

The authors attribute the gap to failures at the start (forgetting, missed opportunities), problems along the way (progress not tracked, competing goals) and early dropout.6 This is not ignorance: it is the organisation of action.

Step 3 of 6 · How long a habit takes

A habit forms over weeks, sometimes months, with large differences

When we say “repeat”, we assume that with enough repetition the action becomes automatic and costs less effort. This is what is called a habit: an action triggered by a context, not by a deliberate decision.11 How many repetitions does it take? The reference study is that of Lally and colleagues: volunteers chose a daily behaviour (drinking, eating, exercising) and rated each day how automatic it felt, for 84 days.10,11

A habit takes weeks, and the duration varies enormously from one person to another

Grey: range of individuals. Blue: middle half (Lally) or range of medians (Singh). Dot: median. Lally: 39 people out of 82 whose curve could be fitted, median for exercise beyond the follow-up period, therefore partly estimated. Singh: medians from only 4 studies.

What this means

The famous figure is 66 days, but it is widely misunderstood. It is the median of the 39 people (out of 82 analysable) whose automaticity curve could be fitted, with durations ranging from 18 to 254 days.10 Water became automatic in 59 days (median), exercise in 91, which is more than the 84 days of follow-up, so partly estimated, and with no significant difference given the small sample.10 For you: plan for months. The “21 days” is a myth stemming from anecdotal observations, as Gardner and colleagues point out.11

The most recent meta-analysis confirms the order of magnitude: Singh and colleagues pooled 20 studies (2,601 participants). In the 4 studies that reported a time, medians ranged from 59 to 66 days, means from 106 to 154, and individuals from 4 to 335 days.12 A caution: 11 of the 20 studies had a high risk of bias, and physical activity was only one of the behaviours studied (along with diet, flossing and others).12

Two practical points emerge. A stable context matters: behaviours done at the same time and chosen by the person consolidated better, with morning routines being more resistant.12,26 And missing one day does not break everything: in Lally, one missed opportunity did not notably disrupt progress, which says nothing about several misses in a row.10,11

What this means

This is the core of the “patience and repetition” thesis, and it is largely confirmed: ease comes with repetition in a stable context, and it takes weeks to months. What these studies do not say is that patience is a trait. They say that repetition can be programmed: a cue, a time, a place.

Three levers have been studied for sticking with it during those weeks when it does not happen by itself: a precise plan, measurement, and the people around you.

Step 4 of 6 · What helps you repeat

Precise plans, measurement and the people around you help, with modest effects

Deciding in advance when and where

An “implementation intention”, or “if... then” plan, links a specific situation to a specific action: “If it's Tuesday at 18 h when I leave the office, then I put on my shoes and walk for 25 minutes.” Gollwitzer and Sheeran synthesised 94 studies (8,461 participants): compared with a simple intention, such a plan improves goal attainment (d = 0.65; 0.59 across 23 health studies).8 For physical activity specifically, the meta-analysis by Bélanger-Gravel and colleagues (26 studies) finds a smaller effect: 0.31 just after the intervention and 0.24 at follow-up, with plans being more effective when they set out how to handle obstacles.9

An “if... then” plan helps, a little less for physical activity, a little less still over time

Standardised effect sizes (d). They come from different meta-analyses, on different goals: the order of magnitude can be compared, not the figures to the decimal. The 0.59 “health” figure is taken from a chapter that cites the meta-analysis (not re-read directly).

What this means

A precise plan helps, but it does not work miracles on physical activity, and its effect seems to erode over time (studies with longer follow-up find smaller effects).8 For you: write down the when and the where, and what you do when the foreseeable obstacle arrives (rain, fatigue, travel). The plan gets you started, repetition does the rest.

Measuring and recording

Michie and colleagues coded diet and physical activity interventions (122 evaluations, 44,747 participants). Self-monitoring accounted for the largest share of the differences between studies (13%), and combining it with at least one other control technique gave an effect of 0.42, versus 0.26 for the others.13 Harkin and colleagues, across 138 randomised trials (19,951 participants), show that monitoring your progress increases goal attainment (d = 0.40), with larger effects when progress is physically recorded or made public.14 Consumer wearables give 0.24 on steps and 0.27 on moderate-to-vigorous activity.15

Measuring yourself and recording your sessions is part of what helps you stick with it

Standardised effect sizes, small to medium. The measures are not of the same nature (trials of varied interventions, all goals for Harkin, wearables for Brickwood): read the order of magnitude, not a ranking.

What this means

Recording what you do has a real effect, small to medium, especially when it comes with goals that you adjust. Harkin notes that a very large increase in monitoring frequency (d = 1.98) produces only 0.40 on goal attainment: measuring yourself is not enough.6,14 For you, measurement is an engine provided it changes something: the THW test is the anchor point, and the retest shows whether your sessions are having an effect. Measure little, on the same dates, with the same protocol.

Not being alone

The evidence is thinner and indirect. In a weight-loss programme (not exercise: to be transposed with caution), Wing and Jeffery compared participants recruited alone with others recruited with friends and supported: about 76% versus 95% completed, and 24% versus 66% had kept their weight loss at month 10.16 On the physical activity side, a meta-analysis of 44 studies (4,578 participants) compares group interventions with others: for adherence, truly cohesive groups outperform standard group classes (d = 0.74), but this comparison rests on few effects (10), and only adherence was measured in it.17

What this means

Having someone who knows you are training, a partner or a group, is associated with better follow-through. The effect is plausible, consistent with public monitoring (Harkin), but it comes from heterogeneous trials. For you: arrange at least one witness to whom you send your result every week.

Plans, measurement and the people around you organise the environment rather than willpower. A more ordinary problem remains: the session has to be easy to start and bearable enough that you come back.

Step 5 of 6 · The cost of starting and enjoyment

The more a session costs to start and the less pleasant it is, the less you repeat it

The first cost is time. A review of reviews published in 2024 in the British Journal of Sports Medicine reports that about half of adults state lack of time as a barrier to exercise, and that factors related to time allocation appear in 72% of the 25 reviews examined.18 The authors stress that the time actually taken up by commitments is a poor predictor of the feeling of not having enough: it is partly a question of priority and organisation.18

The second cost is the starting dose. Adherence syntheses associate a very intense start with a high dropout rate.4 The third is how it feels: according to Ekkekakis's dual-mode theory, lower intensities generally provide more pleasure.25 In terms of evidence, Williams and colleagues found that the affective response to a moderate session was associated with participation in physical activity 6 and 12 months later.20 A review of 24 studies (Rhodes and Kates) concludes that a positive affective change during moderate-intensity exercise is linked to future activity, whereas affect after exercise is not.19

When the effort is pleasant, you come back more often

Two small randomised trials, over short periods (8 weeks, 6 months); the second is a pilot trial whose difference is not significant for energy expenditure. The bottom bars use a different unit from the top ones.

What this means

Two trials point the same way, with clear reservations. In Teixeira's trial (46 people, 8 weeks), the group whose intensity was set by pleasure went to the gym 14.35 times versus 8.13 times, about 77% more, and the gap did not narrow over the period.22 Williams's pilot trial (59 people, 6 months) finds about 26 more minutes of walking per week when a self-chosen pace is recommended rather than an imposed moderate intensity.21 Limits: short duration, small samples, supervision. For you: a session you can tolerate is better than a perfect session you avoid. Stay at a comfortable intensity at the start.

What remains is the most honest case to look at: what happens when you have stuck with it, then stop.

Step 6 of 6 · Relapse and objections

Slips are normal, and the starting thesis is a little too simple

A study of 65 long-term exercisers listed what made them miss a session: bad weather, inconvenient schedule, negative emotions, fatigue.23 These situations are foreseeable, therefore plannable: this is the purpose of “if... then” plans.

We must now honestly test the founder's thesis, with three objections.

“Knowing what to do is no longer complicated”

True for the foundation, partly false beyond it. The general recommendations are clear.2 But starting too hard increases dropout, and the starting dose depends on injuries, fitness and contraindications. The difficulty is also to calibrate the start so that it is repeatable.

“Patience is all it takes”

No evidence read shows that a character quality explains sticking with it. They show conditions: a stable cue, a low dose at the start, monitoring, a witness, a bearable effort. Someone who fails has not necessarily lacked patience: they may have had a start that was too hard and nobody to know about it.

“Repeating is all it takes”

Without a retest, you do not know whether repetition is producing anything. The evidence on self-monitoring points that way, but it is not specific to physical activity and its effect is modest.13,14

Answer to the question

Let us return to the question: is the main obstacle knowing what to do, or taking action and sticking with it? What is solid: the knowledge foundation is stable, the gap between wanting and doing is massive (around 46% among people who have the intention), dropping out of a programme is common (about half within six months in the old syntheses), and a habit takes weeks to months to form, with very large individual variation. The thesis is well supported at this level.

What is probable: precise plans, self-monitoring, the people around you and pleasant effort help you stick with it. The measured effects are small to medium, weaker for physical activity than for other goals, and they often rest on participants' own reports.

What is not: that patience is a character trait to be cultivated, that 66 days is a guaranteed duration, that a partner works for everyone, or that knowing what to do is a settled problem for every person. The right formulation is therefore: the foundation is simple, sticking with it is hard, and sticking with it can be organised. It is less appealing than “patience is all it takes”, but it is what the data support.

What we put in place: twelve weeks to stick with it

What follows is a generic proposal, not a personalised programme or medical advice, and it has not been tested as such. Each element rests on evidence cited above, but the assembly is a design choice. It applies to a healthy adult who is starting or restarting. The profile articles specify the starting point, the risks and the obstacles specific to each situation.

Before you start

  • Take the THW test on the page: it is your starting point (week 1). Note the result and the date.
  • Choose an endurance activity you can tolerate and a simple strength session. Write down the day, time and place of each week 1 session, and what you will do if the foreseeable obstacle arrives.9
  • Appoint a witness to whom you will send the number of sessions done each week.14,17
  • Get medical advice before starting if you have a known cardiovascular, metabolic or kidney disease, or symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath at rest or with light effort, dizziness or faintness.24 The reference list is that of the ACSM recommendations (read from a summary), to be completed with your doctor.

A twelve-week trajectory: little at the start, and we measure three times

Programme proposal, not tested as such: the minutes are an example of gradual build-up, to be adjusted. Only the reference line comes from a source (WHO 2020 recommendation, adults, 150 to 300 minutes per week of moderate intensity).

Weeks 1 to 4 proposal

Set up the rhythm, not the performance

  • Dose: about 45 to 60 minutes per week in total, in 3 short sessions (15 to 20 minutes).
  • Typical sessions: 2 easy endurance sessions (brisk walking, cycling, very slow running: you should be able to talk) and 1 full-body strength session with simple movements, few sets.
  • Progression: none on intensity. Only add minutes if you have done all the sessions.
  • Single goal: do not miss a single week. A stable context matters more than the content.11,12

Weeks 5 to 8 proposal

Add dose, keep the same framework

  • Dose: about 80 to 100 minutes per week, in 3 to 4 sessions.
  • Typical sessions: 2 endurance sessions (one of them a little longer), 1 to 2 strength sessions. Add a short mobility or balance routine if your THW test showed a weakness there.
  • Progression: increase only one variable at a time (duration or load), never both.
  • THW retest at week 6: same conditions as week 1, same time of day if possible. Compare with week 1 without drawing conclusions from a single result: a variation in one test can come from fatigue or from how you feel that day.

Weeks 9 to 12 proposal

Reach the recommended foundation

  • Dose: about 120 to 150 minutes per week, reaching the low end of the WHO range (150 minutes).2
  • Typical sessions: 3 endurance sessions, one of them more sustained if you can tolerate it, and 2 strength sessions.
  • THW retest at week 12: compare weeks 1, 6 and 12. An improvement confirms that repetition has an effect. No improvement is a prompt to check your actual consistency, sleep and dose before changing programme.

After week 12: maintenance proposal

  • Keep the same framework (same days, same cue): the habit in Lally and Singh consolidates over months, not over twelve weeks.10,12
  • Retest about every three months, no more often. This interval is a practical choice, not a study result.

When to move forward, when to step back

  • Move forwardGo to the next phase if you have done at least four out of five planned sessions for two weeks in a row, with no persistent pain. This threshold is a design benchmark, not a value from a study.
  • StayIf you missed more than half of the sessions in a week, repeat the same week. Do not add dose to catch up.
  • Step backIf you miss two weeks in a row, go back to the dose of the previous phase and check the “if... then” plan: time, place, likely obstacle. The problem is more often the organisation than the programme.
  • Stop and ask for adviceChest pain, abnormal shortness of breath, dizziness or faintness, joint pain that increases from one session to the next: stop, and see a doctor.24

The five rules of repetition

  1. Start too small to fail.Starting too hard is associated with dropout.4 The Gardner authors recommend starting with small changes and attaching them to an existing routine.11
  2. Hook the session to a fixed cue.Same day, same time, same place, with an “if... then” plan written in advance, including for the foreseeable obstacle.8,9,11
  3. One slip does not count, two in a row do.An isolated miss did not break automaticity in Lally.10 The “never two in a row” rule is a design benchmark: the evidence does not cover several slips in a row.
  4. Measure little, on fixed dates, and record every session.Self-monitoring helps, especially with goals that you review.13,14 Your three THW retests (weeks 1, 6, 12) serve as benchmarks.
  5. Keep the effort bearable, and do not stay alone.Pleasant effort is linked to more sessions, and a witness or a group is associated with better follow-through.17,22

Common mistakes

  • Looking for the perfect programmeChanging programme at the first difficulty resets repetition to zero. This is a logical consequence of the habit results, not a directly tested comparison.
  • Judging yourself on a single dayA test varies with sleep, time of day and how you feel that day. Look at the trend over three measurements.
Profile articles

This foundation is shared. What changes depending on your situation (age, sex, starting point, pain, goals) is covered in the profile articles, which take up this protocol with doses, risks and obstacles specific to each case.

Limits

What the article cannot say
  • The dropout figures come from old syntheses (1991, 1994): a benchmark, not a current measurement.
  • Lally is based on small samples of volunteers, read here from a detailed summary.
  • The effects of plans, self-monitoring, the group and pleasure are modest, drawn from short and partly self-reported trials; the social evidence comes partly from a weight-loss programme.
  • The protocol is a proposal, not tested as it stands, and it replaces neither medical advice nor a coach.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to become a habit?

More than three weeks. The observed medians range from about 59 to 66 days, with individuals from 18 to 335 days depending on the study, and exercise seems to take longer than other simple behaviours (median of 91 days in Lally, with a small sample).10,12 Plan for several months.

Do you have to train flat out for it to count?

No. At the start, a bearable effort is associated with better adherence, and the WHO reminds us that some activity is better than none.2,4

My test score is low: is that a bad start?

It is a starting point. A low score simply leaves more room for progress. The retest will tell you whether repetition has an effect.
